title: AI in Education 15 Five Things I Learnt from Bibi Groot
author: Craig Barton
summary: Craig Barton reports on the second Eedi and Google DeepMind trial of an AI maths tutor, with 1,179 pupils aged 12 to 15 in ten UK schools, randomised across standard remediation, expert human tutors and two AI tutor versions. In-lesson results replicated the first trial: tutored pupils did markedly better on follow-up questions, and the AI matched the human experts. On the broad Star Maths test after ten weeks, however, there was no difference between groups, which Bibi Groot attributes to tutored pupils covering fewer study units. Barton draws a general lesson about judging a new approach on a broad test too early. Further findings include a gender split, in which tutoring helped girls and slightly held boys back, and the AI asking follow-up checks far more often than humans (91 percent against 60 percent). Supervising the AI proved safer, with 94.7 percent of messages accepted unchanged, but tutors found it less enjoyable.
points: The AI tutor matched expert human tutors on every in-lesson measure, with pupils answering similar questions correctly about 57 percent of the time against 43 percent for standard remediation.
The Star Maths result was a null effect, likely because tutored pupils completed a median of 77 to 99 study units against 132, going deeper but covering less.
Boys and girls experienced tutoring differently: the gender gap closed partly because tutoring helped girls and partly because boys saw tutor chats as punishment for mistakes.
The AI asked a follow-up check after a fixed mistake in 91 percent of conversations against 60 percent for humans, which is the habit tutors said they then copied.
Supervising the AI was safer but less engaging for tutors, who reported feeling less enthusiastic and less excited.
quotes: After ten weeks, there was no difference. Students tutored by either version of the AI made the same gains on Star Maths as students who had standard remediation.

Over the ten weeks, students in standard remediation completed a median of 132 study units. Students with an AI tutor completed 99, and students with a human tutor completed 77. A tutoring conversation took four to seven minutes, and human tutors replied more slowly than the AI. Star Maths covers a huge range of topics, so it rewards breadth. Tutored students went deeper, but covered less.
If your department trials a new approach for half a term and then judges it on a broad end-of-year style test, you may well conclude it doesn’t work, when it simply hasn’t had time to show up.

Many of the boys perceived being pulled into a tutor conversation as a punishment for getting a question wrong. And to be fair to them, every single mistake triggered a chat, including the ones where they had simply clicked B when they meant to click C.
The worst check for understanding in the world is “Does that make sense?”, because every child says yes, whether it does or not.
Once a student had fixed their original mistake, the AI asked them a follow-up question to check their understanding in 91% of conversations. The human tutors did this in 60%.
On the AI days, they said the drafts were helpful (82% of diaries) and saved them time (86%), and they felt slightly more confident about the quality of their tutoring.
